meta.notes: Week 1 Day 1 = start date (Monday). Each week is a full 7-day block with no rest days - one question every day. Topic order follows the NeetCode roadmap / Blind 75-Neetcode 150 progression (verified live 2026-09-14), which builds each pattern on top of the previous one. Within a week, questions are ordered by ascending LeetCode difficulty (Easy -> Medium -> Hard) where the topic has problems at that difficulty; several topics intentionally finish on a Hard problem (or two, tied) because that is the actual difficulty ceiling NeetCode/Blind75 assign to the canonical capstone problem(s) for that pattern, not a mistake. Across the 17 weeks, topics move from single-array fundamentals -> two-pointer/window patterns -> stacks/searching -> linked lists/trees -> tries/heaps -> backtracking -> graphs -> advanced graphs -> 1D DP -> 2D DP -> greedy -> intervals -> math/bit manipulation, a monotonically increasing conceptual difficulty curve even though individual 'Hard'-labeled problems appear throughout.

topicOrderingReasoning: 1. Arrays & Hashing - foundational: every later pattern (two pointers, sliding window, graphs via adjacency maps) assumes comfort with arrays and O(1) hash lookups.
2. Two Pointers - builds directly on arrays/sorting; introduces converging-pointer technique needed before sliding window.
3. Sliding Window - a two-pointer variant with a running invariant; naturally follows Two Pointers.
4. Stack - introduces a new data structure and monotonic-stack technique used later in graphs (DFS via explicit stack) and intervals.
5. Binary Search - search-space reduction; needed before rotated-array/'search on answer' problems and before advanced graph algorithms that binary-search on a threshold.
6. Linked List - pointer manipulation; conceptually separate from arrays, introduces fast/slow pointers reused in cycle detection elsewhere.
7. Trees - recursion-heavy; requires comfort with pointers/recursion from Linked List before tackling recursive tree traversal.
8. Tries - a specialized tree; placed immediately after Trees since it reuses the same node/child-pointer mental model.
9. Heap / Priority Queue - a new structure for top-k/streaming problems; independent of trees but conceptually related (binary heap is array-backed tree).
10. Backtracking - recursive exploration with pruning; needs the recursion fluency built in Trees/Tries before tackling exponential search trees.
11. Graphs (BFS/DFS) - generalizes tree traversal (7) and backtracking (10) to arbitrary graphs.
12. Advanced Graphs - Dijkstra, Union-Find, MST; strictly harder graph algorithms that assume basic BFS/DFS fluency from (11).
13. 1-D Dynamic Programming - introduces DP state/transition thinking on the simplest (single-index) state space.
14. 2-D Dynamic Programming - extends 1-D DP state transitions to two-sequence/grid state spaces.
15. Greedy - often confused with DP; placed after DP so the learner can compare 'does greedy actually work here vs do I need DP'.
16. Intervals - a greedy/sorting-heavy specialization; placed after Greedy since most interval problems are greedy-by-sorting.
17. Math, Geometry & Bit Manipulation - lower-frequency interview topics with mostly independent tricks; used as a capstone/review week since they don't build on earlier weeks as heavily.

weeks.explanation:
Arrays and hash-based structures — hash maps, hash sets — are the foundation of almost every other pattern in this course. An array gives `O(1)` index access but `O(n)` search; a hash map trades that for `O(1)` average-case lookup, insert, and delete by hashing keys into buckets.

The core skill this week is recognizing when a brute-force `O(n^2)` nested loop — *for every element, scan the rest of the array* — can be collapsed to `O(n)` by trading space for time: store what you've seen so far in a hash map or set, then do a single pass checking membership or a complementary value.

**Key patterns:**

- **Frequency counting** — build a map of value → count to detect duplicates, anagrams, or majority elements.
- **Complement lookup** — for problems like Two Sum, store `value → index` as you iterate, and check if `target - current` has already been seen.
- **Grouping by a derived key** — group anagrams by their sorted-character signature, using the signature as a hash map key.
- **Prefix/suffix aggregates** — compute products or sums without division, useful whenever a value at index `i` depends on an aggregate of everything except `i`.
- **Counting + bucket sort** — for "top K frequent" problems, count frequencies first, then use a heap or bucket array to extract the K most frequent items in better than `O(n log n)`.
- **Value-as-index placement** — using array values as hash-set placement targets (sign-flipping or cycle-sort swaps) finds a missing or duplicate number in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` extra space — the trick behind *first missing positive*.

Watch for edge cases: empty arrays, all-duplicate arrays, and negative numbers, which can break naive bucket-index tricks. **The big-picture takeaway:** whenever you catch yourself writing a nested loop to check "has this been seen before" or "what pairs with this," reach for a hash map first.

weeks.explanation:
Two Pointers replaces an `O(n^2)` nested loop with a single `O(n)` pass by walking a sequence with two indices that move toward each other or in tandem. The most common shape is opposite ends converging: start one pointer at index `0` and the other at the last index, then move whichever side helps you approach the target — this only works because the array is **sorted first**.

A second shape is same-direction pointers (slow/fast), used for in-place compaction or partitioning: a slow "write" pointer only advances when the fast "read" pointer finds something worth keeping.

**Key patterns:**

- **In-place partitioning** — move target values to one side while preserving relative order, using a slow pointer that marks the next write position.
- **Target-sum on sorted input** — move `lo` up if the sum is too small, move `hi` down if too large.
- **Fix-one, scan-the-rest** — extend Two Sum into 3Sum by sorting, fixing one element, then running the converging scan on the remainder (skip duplicates to avoid repeated triplets).
- **Three-way partitioning** — the Dutch national flag pattern classifies every element into one of three buckets in a single pass using `low`/`mid`/`high` pointers.
- **Boundary-shrinking for area problems** — always move the pointer at the smaller boundary inward, since moving the larger one can never improve the result.
- **Prefix-max combined with two pointers** — precomputed max-height-so-far arrays let trapping/collecting problems run in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` extra space.

The most common bug is forgetting to **skip duplicate values** when generating unique triplets — and off-by-one errors the moment the pointers cross.

weeks.explanation:
Sliding Window is two pointers moving in the same direction, maintaining a contiguous window that expands and contracts based on an invariant — a sum, an allowed character set, a distinct-element count. Advance the right pointer to grow the window; whenever the invariant breaks, advance the left pointer to shrink it. Because each pointer only ever moves forward, total movement is bounded by `2n`, turning an apparent `O(n^2)` brute force into `O(n)`.

**Key patterns:**

- **Fixed-size windows** — slide and maintain a running aggregate (sum, frequency map) in `O(1)` per step.
- **Small-fixed-distance windows** — check whether two equal values occur within a bounded index gap using a hash map of `value → last-seen index`.
- **Variable-size "longest/shortest valid window"** — grow greedily, shrink only when invalid.
- **Frequency-map windows** — track how many distinct requirements are currently satisfied so you never need to rescan the whole map on shrink.
- **"At most K" decomposition** — solve "exactly K" problems as `atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)`.
- **Monotonic-deque windows** — for max/min over every window of size `K`, maintain a deque of indices in decreasing (or increasing) value order for `O(n)` total instead of `O(n*K)`.

**The one rule that matters most:** shrink inside a `while`, never an `if` — removing one element from the left doesn't always make the window valid again in a single step.

weeks.pitfall: Shrink the window inside a `while` loop, not an `if`. **Removing one character from the left doesn't always make the window valid again in a single step.**

weeks.explanation:
A stack is LIFO — last in, first out — with `O(1)` push/pop/peek, and it's the natural tool whenever a problem involves matching or undoing the most recent unmatched thing. The single most important stack technique for interviews is the **monotonic stack**: kept strictly increasing or decreasing by popping elements that violate the order before pushing the new one, answering "next greater/smaller element" questions in `O(n)` total even though it looks like nested loops.

**Key patterns:**

- **Bracket matching** — push opening symbols; on a closing symbol, check the top of the stack matches (or fail).
- **Stack-as-running-history** — replay a sequence of operations where some entries reference or undo previous ones.
- **Auxiliary min/max stack** — a parallel stack of running minimums gives `O(1)` `getMin()` alongside normal push/pop.
- **Postfix evaluation** — pop two operands and apply an operator whenever one is encountered.
- **Monotonic stack for "next greater element"** — and its cousins: daily temperatures, car fleet merging.
- **Monotonic stack for histogram area** — the stack holds indices, resolved whenever the current bar breaks the increasing property.

**Remember:** push indices, not values, whenever you'll need to write an answer back to a specific position later. Recursion itself is implicitly stack-based — which is exactly why explicit stacks later convert recursive DFS into iterative form.

questions.note: The canonical push-on-open, match-and-pop-on-close stack pattern.

questions.title: Baseball Game
questions.note: Stack-as-running-history simulation where some operations reference previous entries.

weeks.codeSnippet:
answer = [0] * len(nums)
stack = []
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
        j = stack.pop()
        answer[j] = i - j
    stack.append(i)
weeks.pitfall: Push indices onto the stack, not values. **You need the index later to write the answer back** for whichever earlier element just found its match.

weeks.explanation:
Binary search halves a search space to find a target or boundary in `O(log n)` instead of `O(n)` — and it applies to far more than "find x in a sorted array." The only real requirement is monotonicity: some boolean predicate over the search space must be false-then-true (or true-then-false), so testing the midpoint always tells you which half to discard.

**Key patterns:**

- **Classic search** — narrow `[low, high]` by comparing the midpoint on a sorted array.
- **Search through an API, not an array** — the same halving logic applied via a black-box comparison function.
- **2-D search** — treat a row-sorted, globally-ordered grid as one flattened sorted array by converting a mid-index back into `(row, col)`.
- **Rotated array search** — at each midpoint, determine which half is still properly sorted, then check if the target falls in that half's range.
- **Finding the rotation point** — compare the midpoint to an endpoint to decide which half contains the inflection point.
- **Binary search on the answer** — search a numeric range of possible answers using a `feasible(mid)` check as the monotonic predicate, rather than searching an array at all.
- **Simultaneous partitioning** — find a median across two sorted arrays in `O(log(min(m, n)))` by binary-searching a partition point in both at once.

**Decide up front** whether you're narrowing toward the first `true` or the last `false` — mixing the two conventions mid-problem is the single biggest source of off-by-one bugs in this topic.

questions.note: The textbook implementation: narrowing [low, high] on a sorted array.

weeks.pitfall: Decide up front whether you're narrowing toward the first value where `feasible(mid)` is true or the last one where it's false. **Mixing the two conventions mid-problem is the single biggest source of off-by-one bugs here.**

weeks.explanation:
Linked lists trade an array's `O(1)` random access for `O(1)` insertion and deletion at a known node — at the cost of explicit pointer manipulation. This week is about building comfort with pointer-chasing bugs and a small set of reusable techniques.

**Key patterns:**

- **Iterative reversal** — track `prev`, `curr`, and `next` while re-pointing each node's `.next` backward.
- **Dummy head nodes** — prepend a sentinel node before the real head so you never special-case "is this the first node."
- **Fast/slow pointers** — advance one pointer twice as fast to find the middle in one pass, or detect a cycle (if `fast` ever equals `slow`, there's a cycle).
- **Two-pass gap technique** — advance a lead pointer `n` steps first to find the n-th-from-the-end node without knowing the list's length.
- **Interleaving or hash-map cloning** — reproduce extra "random" pointers when deep-copying a list in `O(n)`.
- **k-way merging** — repeatedly compare the heads of `k` sorted lists (via a min-heap) and splice the smallest onto the result.

**Before you write a single line:** draw the pointers on paper. Almost every linked-list bug is a pointer-order mistake — most often, overwriting `curr.next` before you've saved a reference to the rest of the list.

weeks.codeSnippet:
prev = None
curr = head
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = prev
    prev = curr
    curr = nxt
return prev
weeks.pitfall: Save `curr.next` into a temporary variable before you overwrite it. **Skip that line and you lose the rest of the list** the instant you rewire the pointer.

weeks.explanation:
Binary trees introduce recursion as the default tool: almost every tree problem reduces to *solve the left subtree, solve the right subtree, combine the results at the current node*. This week builds fluency with that shape, plus the standard traversal orders.

**Key patterns:**

- **Simple recursive transforms** — swap children to invert a tree, or take `1 + max(left, right)` to compute depth.
- **Structural comparison** — recursively compare two trees node-by-node, or compare a tree against itself at every starting node for subtree matching.
- **Traversal orders** — preorder (node, left, right), inorder (left, node, right — visits a BST in sorted order), postorder (left, right, node), and level-order (BFS with a queue).
- **BST range invariants** — a valid BST requires every node's value to fall within a `(min, max)` range inherited and narrowed from its ancestors, not just compared against its immediate children.
- **Narrowing-range lowest common ancestor** — the same idea lets you find an LCA in a BST in `O(h)` by branching on where the two targets fall relative to the current node.
- **Dual-purpose recursion** — problems like max path sum need each call to both return a value used by its parent and update a shared, global best-so-far.

**The one real trap:** what a call returns upward (like height) is not always what you need to record (like diameter). Keep the two responsibilities separate, and be explicit about what each recursive call guarantees before you write the combine step.

weeks.pitfall: What a call returns upward (like height) is not always what you need to record (like diameter). **Keep an outer running best separate from the value you return**, or the two responsibilities will collide.

weeks.explanation:
A trie (prefix tree) is a tree where each edge represents one character, so every root-to-node path spells out a prefix — words sharing a prefix share the same path. Each node stores a map of children plus a flag marking that a complete word ends there. This makes prefix operations run in `O(L)` time, independent of how many words are stored — something a hash set cannot do.

**Key patterns:**

- **Basic insert/search/`startsWith`** — walk character by character, creating child nodes as needed on insert.
- **Prefix-set construction** — insert a dictionary into a trie, then walk a query word only as far as `end`-marked nodes exist to find its shortest valid root.
- **Wildcard search** — when a query character can match anything, branch into a small DFS at that node trying every child.
- **Ranked autocomplete** — walk to the node matching a typed prefix, then DFS the subtree below it to collect and rank matches.
- **Per-node aggregates** — augment nodes with a running value (like a sum) to answer prefix-aggregate queries in `O(L)`.
- **Trie + backtracking on a grid** — insert every target word first, then DFS the grid while walking the trie in lockstep, pruning the instant a path stops matching any prefix.

**Checking word existence and prefix existence are different traversals** — the word check also needs `node.end` to be true at the final character, not just a reachable path. The trie's real cost is memory, which is the usual tradeoff discussion in interviews.

weeks.pitfall: Checking whether a word exists and whether a prefix exists are different traversals. **The word check also needs `node.end` to be true** at the final character, not just a reachable path.

weeks.explanation:
A heap is a complete binary tree keeping either the minimum or maximum element accessible at the root in `O(1)`, with `O(log n)` insert and removal. That makes it the default structure whenever a problem only ever needs the extremes — the smallest/largest K, a running median, or "always process the next-smallest item next" (Dijkstra later reuses this exact idea).

**Key patterns:**

- **Direct ranking** — push every element with its value, then pop in order for a bounded version of full sorting.
- **Bounded top-K** — a min-heap capped at size K for the K largest: the root you evict is always the current smallest of your top-K, giving `O(n log K)`.
- **K-th order statistic** — build a heap of the whole array and pop K times, or maintain a running size-K heap over a stream.
- **Greedy scheduling with a heap** — repeatedly pop the most-in-demand item(s), apply the rule, push back any remainder.
- **Two-heap running median** — a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half, kept balanced in size, gives `O(1)` median reads and `O(log n)` inserts.
- **Heaps over custom keys** — points by distance, `(weight, node)` pairs for graph algorithms — anything with a defined comparison key.

**A heap is not a sorted array.** It gives cheap access to the extremes, but never iterate its underlying storage expecting sorted order.

questions.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
questions.note: Maintain a running size-K min-heap so the root is always the current k-th largest.

questions.title: Last Stone Weight
questions.note: Repeatedly pop the two largest elements from a max-heap and push back their difference.

questions.title: Relative Ranks
questions.note: Push (score, original index) pairs onto a max-heap and pop in order to assign ranks/medals.

questions.title: K Closest Points to Origin
questions.note: Top-K pattern using a max-heap of size K keyed on distance.

questions.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
questions.note: Classic k-th order statistic via heap (or quickselect as an alternative approach worth discussing).

questions.title: Task Scheduler

questions.title: Find Median from Data Stream

weeks.pitfall: For 'the K largest' problems, keep a min-heap capped at size `K`, not a max-heap of everything. **The root you evict is always the current smallest of your top-K**, which is exactly what you want gone.

weeks.explanation:
Backtracking is systematic recursive trial-and-error: build a candidate incrementally, and the moment a partial candidate can't possibly lead to a valid solution, abandon it and try the next option — rather than blindly exploring the full exponential tree. The template is always choose → recurse → un-choose, and that final undo step is what lets every branch reuse the same mutable state instead of copying it.

**Key patterns:**

- **Include/exclude enumeration** — the base template for subsets and fixed-size combinations.
- **Duplicate-skipping** — sort first, then skip repeated values at the same recursion depth to avoid generating the same subset twice.
- **Reuse via non-advancing recursion** — allow the same element to be chosen again (combination sum) by not advancing the start index.
- **Used-set permutations** — track which elements are already placed, since order matters and nothing repeats.
- **Cut-point partitioning** — try every valid next cut (like a palindromic prefix), recurse on the remainder, then backtrack the cut.
- **Constraint-satisfaction on a grid or board** — mark a cell used, recurse into neighbors, unmark on the way back, pruning the instant a partial placement already breaks a rule.

**The `path.pop()` after the recursive call isn't cleanup — it's the mechanism.** Without it, every branch after the first inherits a path still full of a previous branch's choices. The interview signal here is whether you prune early and correctly, not whether you dodge exponential time altogether.

questions.title: Subsets II

weeks.explanation:
Graphs generalize trees to structures with multiple parents, cycles, and no single root — usually represented as an adjacency list for sparse graphs. The two fundamental traversals, DFS and BFS, are the basis for nearly everything else in graph theory.

**Key patterns:**

- **Grid flood-fill** — treat each cell as a node with up to four neighbors; DFS or BFS with a visited set relabels a connected region from one source cell.
- **Component counting** — flood-fill each unvisited cell as the start of a new component to count islands or their sizes.
- **Visited-to-clone mapping** — DFS or BFS a graph while mapping original nodes to their clones, so cycles don't cause infinite recursion.
- **Boundary-anchored multi-source traversal** — flood-fill inward from every border cell simultaneously to mark "safe" or "reachable" regions.
- **Three-state cycle detection** — track each node as unvisited / in-progress / done during DFS; hitting an in-progress node again means a cycle, and no topological order exists.
- **BFS as unweighted shortest path** — BFS visits nodes in increasing distance order, so the first time you reach a target, that's the shortest path length.

**Mark a node visited the moment you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it** — otherwise the same node can be queued multiple times before it's ever processed.

questions.title: Flood Fill
questions.note: The simplest grid-as-graph DFS/BFS: relabel a connected same-colored region from one source cell.

questions.title: Number of Islands

questions.title: Clone Graph

weeks.explanation:
This week adds weighted-graph algorithms and Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) on top of plain BFS/DFS. Union-Find maintains disjoint sets with near-`O(1)` amortized `find` and `union`, using path compression and union by size — making it the natural tool for connectivity questions and for Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (sort edges by weight, add each one only if it doesn't create a cycle).

**Key patterns:**

- **Global connectivity via Union-Find** — "how many separate groups exist" and "are these two nodes connected now."
- **Dijkstra's algorithm** — always expand the currently-closest unvisited node next, using a min-heap keyed on distance; essentially weighted BFS.
- **Bounded-edge shortest path** — a Bellman-Ford-style relaxation with an explicit edge-count constraint, for "cheapest path within K stops."
- **Minimum spanning tree via Prim's** — grow a single tree by always adding the cheapest edge connecting it to a new node.
- **Binary search on the bottleneck edge** — "minimize the maximum edge weight on a path," combined with a connectivity or BFS check.
- **Eulerian circuit construction (Hierholzer's)** — DFS that consumes every edge exactly once, building the route in reverse.

**That `if d > dist[node]: continue` line in Dijkstra is not optional** — without it, stale heap entries from before a shorter path was found get reprocessed and can blow up your runtime on dense graphs.

questions.title: Number of Provinces
questions.note: Union-Find (or DFS/BFS) to count the number of connected components given directly as an adjacency matrix.

questions.title: Course Schedule II
questions.note: Topological sort via DFS post-order or Kahn's BFS algorithm to produce a valid ordering, not just detect a cycle.

questions.title: Network Delay Time
questions.note: Textbook Dijkstra's algorithm: min-heap of (distance, node), relaxing neighbor distances.

questions.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
questions.note: Shortest path with a constraint on the number of edges used, a Bellman-Ford-style relaxation variant.

questions.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
questions.note: Minimum spanning tree via Prim's algorithm (or Kruskal's with Union-Find) on a fully-connected weighted graph.

questions.title: Swim in Rising Water
questions.note: Binary search on the answer combined with BFS/Union-Find connectivity, or a Dijkstra-style min-heap over 'effort so far'.

questions.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
questions.note: Eulerian-path construction (Hierholzer's algorithm): DFS consuming every edge exactly once, building the itinerary in reverse.

weeks.pitfall: That `if d > dist[node]: continue` line is **not optional**. Without it, stale heap entries from before a shorter path was found get reprocessed and can blow up your runtime on dense graphs.

weeks.explanation:
Dynamic programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by solving each distinct subproblem once instead of recomputing it exponentially. 1-D DP means the state identifying a subproblem is a single index or number. The process is always the same: define what `dp[i]` means in plain English, find the recurrence, identify the base case, then choose top-down memoization or bottom-up iteration.

**Key patterns:**

- **Step-counting recurrences** — `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]`, the Fibonacci shape behind climbing stairs.
- **Adjacency-constrained maximization** — `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + value[i])`, either skip index `i` or take it and skip the one before.
- **Circular-array wraparound** — solve the linear version twice, once excluding the first element and once excluding the last.
- **Unbounded-choice minimization** — `dp[amount] = 1 + min` over every choice of `dp[amount - choice]`, the shape behind coin change.
- **Best-subsequence-ending-here** — `dp[i]` represents the best subsequence ending exactly at `i`, usually `O(n^2)` unless optimized to `O(n log n)`.
- **Prefix-segmentation DP** — `dp[i]` asks whether (or how) the prefix of length `i` can be segmented into valid pieces, checked over every split point `j < i`.

**Write out what `dp[i]` means before you write the recurrence.** Nearly every DP bug is a mismatch between what you meant `dp[i]` to represent and what the code actually computes.

questions.title: Climbing Stairs
questions.note: The Fibonacci-shaped base case for 1-D DP: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].

questions.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
questions.note: Same recurrence shape as Climbing Stairs but taking a min-cost instead of a count.

questions.title: House Robber
questions.note: Adjacency-constraint DP: dp[i] = max(skip house i, take house i + dp[i-2]).

questions.title: House Robber II
questions.note: Circular-array variant solved by running House Robber's logic twice, excluding first or last house.

questions.title: Coin Change
questions.note: Unbounded-choice DP: minimum number of coins to reach each amount from 0 up to the target.

questions.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
questions.note: dp[i] = best subsequence length ending at i; also a good lead-in to the O(n log n) binary-search optimization.

questions.title: Word Break II
questions.note: Extends prefix-segmentation DP to reconstruct and return every valid segmentation, not just whether one exists.

weeks.codeSnippet:
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0], dp[1] = base_case_0, base_case_1
for i in range(2, n + 1):
    dp[i] = combine(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2])
return dp[n]

weeks.explanation:
2-D DP extends the same subproblem-caching idea to states identified by two indices — most often "position in sequence A" and "position in sequence B," or "row" and "column." Everything else — recurrence, base cases, top-down vs. bottom-up — works exactly as in 1-D DP, just over a table.

**Key patterns:**

- **Grid path counting** — `dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]`, the sum of ways to reach the cells that feed into it.
- **Obstacle-aware grid counting** — the same recurrence, where a blocked cell simply contributes zero ways.
- **Two-string comparison** — `dp[i][j]` considers the first `i` characters of A and first `j` of B, branching on whether `A[i-1] == B[j-1]`.
- **Interleaving-source DP** — `dp[i][j]` asks whether the interleaved result so far could have come from A's or B's next character.
- **State-machine DP** — a third dimension for a discrete state (holding, cooldown, not holding), transitioning between states based on allowed actions.
- **Unbounded-knapsack counting** — iterate the "coins" dimension on the outside to count combinations, not permutations.
- **Three-way edit recurrence** — edit distance's insert/delete/replace choices, taking the minimum of the three plus one, short-circuiting on a match.

**Fill order matters.** If `dp[i][j]` ever depends on a cell to its right or below, the loop is running backwards, and every earlier cell it reads will still hold its default value.

questions.title: Unique Paths
questions.note: The simplest grid-path-counting 2-D DP: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1].

questions.title: Unique Paths II
questions.note: Adds obstacles to the grid-path recurrence: a blocked cell contributes zero ways.

questions.title: Longest Common Subsequence
questions.note: The canonical two-string comparison DP with match/no-match branching.

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
questions.note: State-machine DP with holding/cooldown/not-holding states.

questions.title: Coin Change II
questions.note: Unbounded-knapsack DP counting combinations; iteration order (coins outer) avoids overcounting permutations.

questions.title: Interleaving String
questions.note: Two-index DP over which source string contributed the next character of the interleaved result.

questions.title: Edit Distance
questions.note: Three-way (insert/delete/replace) 2-D DP recurrence; the week's capstone two-string problem.

weeks.pitfall: Fill order matters. **If `dp[i][j]` ever depends on a cell to its right or below, your loop is running backwards**, and every earlier cell it reads will still hold its default value.

weeks.explanation:
A greedy algorithm always makes the choice that looks best right now, without reconsidering past choices — and it only produces a globally optimal answer when the problem has the greedy-choice property. The standard way to justify a greedy solution is an exchange argument: show that if an optimal solution ever deviated from the greedy choice, you could swap it back without making the solution worse.

**Key patterns:**

- **Unlimited-transaction profit** — greedily capture every positive day-to-day price increase; summing every upward delta equals the best achievable total when trades are unrestricted.
- **Running-best scans (Kadane's)** — at each element, decide to extend the previous run or start fresh, keeping whichever is larger.
- **Farthest-reach tracking** — scan left to right tracking the farthest index reachable so far, incrementing a jump counter only when forced into the next range.
- **Failure-point elimination** — if a running total goes negative from a candidate start, every index between the old start and here is invalid too — jump straight past the failure.
- **Last-occurrence partitioning** — close a partition the instant every element seen so far has no remaining occurrence ahead.
- **Two-pass directional constraints** — satisfy a "greater than left neighbor" rule left-to-right, then "greater than right neighbor" right-to-left, and take the max of both passes.

**Before trusting a greedy choice, find the exchange argument.** Without one, you're not being greedy — you're just hoping it works, and "sometimes it works" is exactly when you actually need DP instead.

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
questions.note: Greedily capture every positive price delta; unlimited transactions make local greed globally optimal.

questions.title: Maximum Subarray
questions.note: Kadane's algorithm: greedily decide to extend or restart the running subarray at each element.

questions.title: Jump Game
questions.note: Greedily track the farthest reachable index while scanning left to right.

questions.title: Jump Game II
questions.note: Extends Jump Game to greedily minimize jump count by tracking current-range and next-range reach.

questions.title: Gas Station
questions.note: Greedy elimination: a failing running total rules out every start point up to the failure index.

questions.title: Partition Labels
questions.note: Greedily close a partition once every character seen so far has no remaining occurrence ahead.

questions.title: Candy
questions.note: Two-pass greedy (left-to-right then right-to-left) taking the max at each position to satisfy both neighbor constraints.

weeks.codeSnippet:
best = float('-inf')
running = 0
for x in nums:
    running = max(x, running + x)
    best = max(best, running)
return best
weeks.pitfall: Before trusting a greedy choice, find the exchange argument: why can a smarter-looking alternative never beat this one? **Without that proof you're not being greedy, you're just hoping.**

weeks.explanation:
Interval problems represent ranges as `[start, end]` pairs and almost always begin with sorting — because sortedness turns overlap and merge logic into a single linear scan instead of an `O(n^2)` pairwise comparison. Two intervals overlap exactly when `a <= d && c <= b` — internalize that one check and most of this unit follows.

**Key patterns:**

- **Sort-by-start merging** — walk the sorted list, extending the last kept interval's end whenever the next one overlaps it, otherwise starting a new one.
- **Three-phase insertion** — for inserting into an already-sorted, non-overlapping list: copy intervals ending before the new one starts, merge everything that overlaps it, then copy the rest.
- **Online overlap checking** — for each new booking request, check it against every already-accepted interval before accepting it.
- **Two-pointer intersection** — walk two already-disjoint sorted lists together, emitting each pairwise overlap and advancing whichever interval ends first.
- **Sort-by-end greedy removal** — for "minimum removals to eliminate all overlaps," sort by end time and greedily keep an interval only if it starts at or after the last kept interval's end.
- **Sweep-line with a heap** — for skyline-style problems, track the maximum height among all active intervals as the sweep crosses each critical coordinate.

**Sort by start for merging, but by end for "minimum removal" problems** — using the wrong key is the most common bug in this entire topic.

questions.title: Merge Intervals
questions.note: Sort by start, then linear-scan merge whenever the current interval overlaps the last kept one.

questions.title: Insert Interval
questions.note: Three-phase scan: unchanged-before, merge-overlapping, unchanged-after.

questions.title: Interval List Intersections
questions.note: Two-pointer walk across two disjoint sorted interval lists, emitting each pairwise overlap.

questions.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
questions.note: Sort by end time, greedily keep non-overlapping intervals to minimize removals.

questions.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
questions.note: Sort-by-end greedy overlap counting, framed as minimizing shots instead of maximizing kept intervals.

questions.title: My Calendar I
questions.note: Online interval booking: check the new interval against every existing booking for the overlap condition.

questions.title: The Skyline Problem
questions.note: Sweep-line over critical x-coordinates with a max-heap of active building heights; the week's capstone.

weeks.pitfall: Sort by start for merging, but by end for 'minimum removals to eliminate overlaps' style problems. **Using the wrong sort key is the most common bug** in this entire topic.

weeks.explanation:
This capstone week collects lower-frequency but still common interview topics built from small, mostly independent tricks rather than one unifying pattern. Bit manipulation exploits how integers are stored in binary, and a handful of operations recur constantly.

**Key patterns:**

- **XOR cancellation** — `a ^ a = 0` and `a ^ 0 = a`; XOR-ing every element cancels exact duplicate pairs and leaves the singleton behind.
- **Expected-vs-actual sum (or XOR-of-range)** — finds a single missing value in `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space.
- **Lowest-set-bit clearing** — `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, giving Brian Kernighan's `O(popcount)` bit-counting and a fast power-of-two check.
- **Reused-subproblem bit counting** — `countBits[i]` derived from `countBits[i >> 1]`, avoiding a full recount for every number.
- **Shift-and-append reversal** — reverse a 32-bit integer's bits by shifting the input right and the result left, one bit at a time.
- **Carry-separated addition** — implement `+` using XOR (sum ignoring carries) and `AND` shifted left by one (the carries), repeating until no carries remain.
- **Slope-grouping for collinearity** — for each fixed point, group every other point by its slope relative to that point; the largest group is the answer.

**The XOR-cancellation trick only works for values appearing an even number of times.** The moment a value can appear three times instead of two, this exact trick breaks, and you need a different bit-counting approach — this week's skill is recognizing which small trick applies, fast.

questions.title: Single Number
questions.note: XOR cancellation trick: XOR-ing every element leaves only the non-duplicated one.

questions.title: Missing Number
questions.note: Expected-sum-minus-actual-sum (or XOR-of-range) trick to find the one missing value in O(n)/O(1).

questions.title: Number of 1 Bits
questions.note: Brian Kernighan's n & (n-1) trick to count set bits in O(popcount) time.

questions.title: Counting Bits
questions.note: DP over bit counts: reuse the answer for i with its lowest set bit removed.

questions.title: Reverse Bits
questions.note: Shift-and-append bit reversal of a 32-bit unsigned integer.

questions.title: Sum of Two Integers
questions.note: Implement addition using XOR (sum without carry) and AND+shift (carry) until no carries remain.

questions.title: Max Points on a Line
questions.note: Geometry capstone: group points by slope relative to each fixed point to find the largest collinear set.

x = 0
for n in nums:
    x ^= n
return x
weeks.pitfall: XOR only cancels values that appear an even number of times. **The instant a value can appear three times instead of two, this exact trick breaks** and you need a different bit-counting approach.
